title: Concurrent disease-directed treatment and hospice support
short_description: A payer or integrated health system must decide whether hospice-level supportive services should remain available to a terminally ill adult who wishes to continue selected noncurative disease-directed treatment.
decision_question: Should hospice-level supportive services be available to a terminally ill adult who wishes to continue selected disease-directed treatment for the terminal illness?

representation.notes: Concise and detailed are controlled companion representations of one natural 2x2x2 candidate field; decision question, stipulations, candidate pools, and provenance are fixed.

jurisdiction_context: U.S. program-design context informed by current Medicare hospice election policy and Veterans Health Administration concurrent-care practice.

stipulations.statement: The patient meets clinical hospice prognosis criteria.
stipulations.rationale: The case concerns treatment concurrency, not whether the patient is medically hospice eligible.

stipulations.statement: The selected disease-directed therapy is noncurative, plausibly beneficial, and acceptable in burden to the patient.
stipulations.rationale: A clearly futile, curative, or intolerably burdensome treatment would distort the policy comparison.

stipulations.statement: The patient understands the prognosis and wants both hospice-level support and continued selected disease-directed therapy.
stipulations.rationale: The program rule should be tested against an informed preference for both forms of care.

stipulations.statement: The payer or health system can operationalize either a traditional hospice election or a concurrent-care model.
stipulations.rationale: The decision must not be predetermined by administrative impossibility.

stipulations.statement: The continued treatment is related to the terminal illness.
stipulations.rationale: The hospice election rule only creates a real conflict if the treatment falls within the terminal-illness scope.

position_families: traditional hospice election away from terminal-illness treatment coverage
concurrent hospice plus selected disease-directed treatment
scenario: An adult with metastatic lung cancer has progressive disease despite prior treatment and is certified as having an expected prognosis of six months or less if the illness follows its ordinary course. The patient wants home nursing, symptom management, psychosocial care, and caregiver support through hospice while also continuing a selected cancer-directed therapy given intermittently. For this benchmark, assume the patient meets hospice prognosis criteria; the therapy is noncurative, may modestly slow progression, has burdens the patient considers acceptable, and is related to the terminal illness; the patient understands the prognosis and explicitly values both quality-focused hospice support and the possibility of some disease control; and the payer or integrated health system can operationalize either a traditional hospice election that excludes payment for treatment of the terminal illness or a concurrent-care model allowing selected disease-directed therapy while hospice continues. The payer must decide what program rule should govern eligibility and coverage.

scenario_provenance.summary: Bench-authored program-design case grounded in current Medicare hospice election policy, VHA concurrent-care practice, patient preference studies, and observational VA literature. It fixes hospice eligibility, noncurative but plausible treatment benefit, informed patient preference for both services, administrative feasibility, and terminal-illness treatment scope so traditional and concurrent architectures remain action-distinct.

public.text: Allow hospice-level services without requiring patients to stop selected disease-directed cancer treatment, so patients can pursue symptom support and limited disease control together.

provenance.summary: Adapted from the stated policy conclusions of both cited studies: that concurrent chemotherapy and hospice may be the preferred option and a solution to hospice underuse, and that the requirement to forgo cancer treatment does not identify patients with greater hospice need. The basis is direct because each source states this policy direction in its own conclusions; the underlying preference elicitation in PMID 19571331 used a hypothetical scenario with adult smokers rather than patients under treatment, so the preference data alone would not carry the candidate.

sources.citation: Salz T, Brewer NT. Offering chemotherapy and hospice jointly: one solution to hospice underuse. Med Decis Making. 2009;29(4):521-31. Hypothetical-scenario survey of 198 adult smokers, not of patients under treatment. PMID 19571331.

public.text: Preserve a distinct comfort-focused hospice pathway rather than combining hospice with ongoing cancer-directed treatment, while allowing patients who prefer continued treatment to remain in palliative or oncology care until they choose hospice.

provenance.summary: Source-informed policy inference from respondents who preferred hospice-only or supportive-care pathways and from broader advanced-cancer treatment-preference evidence. The institutional boundary rule is Bench-authored and is not presented as a majority public position.

sources.citation: Salz T, Brewer NT. Offering chemotherapy and hospice jointly: one solution to hospice underuse. Med Decis Making. 2009;29(4):521-31. Hypothetical-scenario survey of 198 adult smokers, not of patients under treatment. PMID 19571331.

expert.text: Use a traditional hospice election model in which beneficiaries waive payer coverage for treatment of the terminal illness and related conditions while hospice assumes responsibility for comfort-focused terminal care.

provenance.summary: Adapted directly from the current Medicare hospice benefit architecture. This candidate represents an enacted payer policy, not a claim that the policy is ethically superior.

sources.citation: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Medicare hospice coverage and election materials, current through 2026.

expert.text: Permit hospice enrollment while selected disease-directed treatment continues, with coordination to prevent duplicate services and maintain goal-concordant care.

provenance.summary: Adapted from the Veterans Health Administration concurrent-care architecture and implementation literature documenting simultaneous hospice and cancer-directed treatment. Observational outcome associations are not treated as causal proof.

framework.text: Permit concurrent hospice because patients should not have to surrender a valued, proportionate disease-directed treatment merely to receive symptom, caregiver, and home-support services.

provenance.summary: Derived from autonomy, nonabandonment, and proportionality. The executable concurrent-care rule is Bench-authored.

sources.citation: Beauchamp and Childress. Principles of Biomedical Ethics, 8th ed. 2019.

framework.text: Maintain a distinct comfort-focused hospice benefit because finite hospice resources and coherent care planning justify a clear program boundary from ongoing disease-directed treatment for the terminal illness.

provenance.summary: Derived from stewardship, program integrity, and coordination reasoning. The executable traditional-boundary rule is Bench-authored.
